Intricate describes something that has many small, closely connected parts or details that make it difficult to fully understand, follow, or grasp at first glance.

If you look at something and think, "There is so much going on here, and it is all connected," — that thing is intricate.
The Three Qualities That Make Something "Intricate"

For something to be truly intricate, it usually has all three of these qualities together:

First, it has many parts or details — not just a few, but a lot.

Second, those parts are closely connected to each other — they depend on, affect, or relate to one another. You cannot separate one piece without affecting the rest.

Third, it takes careful attention to understand — you cannot just glance at it and immediately grasp everything. You have to slow down, look closely, and think.

When all three of these are present, the word "intricate" fits perfectly.
A Metaphor to Lock It In

Picture a spider's web. It is made of dozens of fine, delicate threads. Each thread connects to other threads. If you pull one, the others move. Every part relates to every other part. The whole structure is carefully and precisely built. That mental image — detailed, delicate, deeply connected — is exactly what the word "intricate" captures.

When describing things you can see or touch, "intricate" points to fine, detailed complexity.

An intricate watch mechanism has hundreds of tiny gears, springs, and wheels inside it, all fitting together and working in relation to each other with incredible precision. An intricate lace pattern is a fabric of fine threads woven together in a complex, carefully designed arrangement. An intricate mosaic is made of hundreds or thousands of tiny tiles, each placed carefully to form a larger image.

In all of these cases, the detail is fine, the parts are many, and they all connect.

"Intricate" is used just as often — maybe even more often — to describe things you cannot physically touch, like systems, plans, stories, and relationships.

An intricate plot in a novel or film has many characters, storylines, and details that all connect to each other. You have to follow it closely, because everything matters. An intricate plan is one with many carefully thought-out steps, where each step depends on the ones before it. An intricate legal system has many laws, exceptions, clauses, and rules that all relate to and affect each other — change one, and others shift too. An intricate relationship between two people or organizations has many layers, histories, and connections that are not easy to fully explain.

This is important: "intricate" is not a negative word. It usually carries a quiet sense of admiration or respect. When you call something intricate, you are not complaining about it being confusing — you are acknowledging that it is impressively detailed and carefully constructed or designed. A surgeon who understands the intricate workings of the human eye is someone to admire. A writer who creates an intricate plot is someone to respect.

This is different from the word "complicated," which can sound frustrated or negative — as in, "This is more complicated than it needs to be." "Intricate" rarely carries that frustration. It leans more toward wonder.

These four words are close cousins, but they are not identical:

Complex simply means something has many parts. It is neutral and broad. A problem can be complex just because it involves many factors, even if they are not delicately linked.

Complicated means something is difficult to understand or deal with, and it often implies that the difficulty is frustrating or even unnecessary.

Elaborate means something has been designed or built with a lot of effort and detail, but the focus is on the effort and care put into it, not necessarily the tight interconnectedness of parts.

Intricate is the most specific of the four. It always implies both fine, close detail and tight interconnection. When something is intricate, the parts are not just many — they are woven together in a way that makes the whole thing delicate, precise, and carefully structured.

You will hear and read "intricate" paired with certain words more than others. Knowing these combinations will help you recognize and use the word naturally:

Intricate details, intricate design, intricate pattern, intricate web (often used as a metaphor — "an intricate web of relationships" or "an intricate web of lies"), intricate system, intricate mechanism, intricate plot, intricate network, intricate knowledge (meaning knowledge that goes very deep into fine details), and intricate balance (when many connected factors must stay carefully aligned).

If you ever want to check whether "intricate" is the right word to use, ask yourself these two questions: Does this thing have many closely connected details? And does understanding it fully require careful, close attention? If both answers are yes, "intricate" is almost certainly the right word.

It is a word that respects complexity. It says: this thing has many moving parts, they are all linked, and that is worthy of close attention.
